passage: I'm Neelam, Zubin's older sister. Every morning he looks at the picture chart on the door: shoes, bag, water bottle. Last month Mummy had to remind him five times. Now he points at each picture and says "done" as he goes. Today he forgot the bottle, but stopped at the door, looked back at the chart and ran to get it. I don't know if he's proud, but he walks out very tall.

qa.q: What pictures are on Zubin's chart?
qa.a: Shoes, bag and water bottle are on the chart.

qa.q: What might Zubin walking out tall suggest?
qa.a: It might suggest he feels proud of finishing his routine by himself.

qa.q: What helps Zubin remember the steps?
qa.a: The picture chart on the door, which he checks and says "done" at each step.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Zubin's progress?
qa.a: She sees he needs far fewer reminders now and can catch his own mistakes.

grounding: An older sister observes a child completing a multi-step routine with few reminders.

passage:
The school bus horn honked earlier than usual. "Varun, the bus is here!" Gurpreet called.
Varun sat up from his puzzle. Shoes first. He pulled them on, velcro rip-rip. Bag next, from the hook. Water bottle last, from the fridge. He ran to the door.
"Wait, your tiffin!" Gurpreet held it out.
Varun grabbed it. "I got three things!"
"And I got the fourth. Go!"

qa.q: Where did Varun get his water bottle from?
qa.a: He got it from the fridge.

qa.q: How can you tell Varun felt pleased with himself?
qa.a: He proudly shouted "I got three things!" as he grabbed the tiffin.

qa.q: How could Gurpreet help Varun remember the tiffin next time?
qa.a: She could add a tiffin picture to his routine so it becomes the fourth step.

qa.q: What would change if the bus had come at the usual time?
qa.a: Varun would have had more time and might have remembered the tiffin too.

grounding: It shows a child following a multi-step routine under time pressure.

passage:
On the fridge of their Chennai flat was Salma's picture chart: shoes, bag, water bottle, a door.

At seven-thirty, Salma, five, stood in front of it. She sat and pulled on her shoes. She grabbed her school bag from the hook. Then she stopped, frowning at the chart. "Water bottle!" She ran to the kitchen.

Her brother Pranav, waiting by the door, didn't say a word. Salma touched the door picture and then the real door. "Ready!"

"All by yourself," Pranav said, grinning.

qa.q: What pictures were on Salma's chart?
qa.a: The chart showed shoes, bag, water bottle and a door.

qa.q: How did Salma feel when she said "Ready!"?
qa.a: She felt proud and pleased that she had done every step by herself.

qa.q: Why did the picture chart help Salma?
qa.a: It showed each step in order, so she could check it herself instead of needing reminders.

qa.q: What is it like for Pranav to wait without reminding her?
qa.a: He may feel tempted to hurry her, but staying quiet lets her succeed on her own, which he clearly enjoys.

grounding: Shows a young child completing a multi-step morning routine with a picture chart and few reminders.

passage:
"Bhupen, what do you need before park?" Sonali asked.

"Shoes!" Bhupen, six, pulled them on.

"Then?"

"Cap. And... bottle!" He fetched both.

"And?"

He thought hard. "Ball!"

"And one more."

Bhupen looked around. Then he ran to the bathroom. "Wash hands first! No, that's after park."

Sonali laughed. "Right, after. So, shoes, cap, bottle, ball. Let's go."

"I remembered almost everything," he said proudly.

qa.q: What did Bhupen say should happen after the park?
qa.a: He said washing hands comes after the park.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel about remembering the steps?
qa.a: He felt proud, saying he remembered almost everything.

qa.q: How could Sonali help Bhupen remember with fewer prompts next time?
qa.a: Sonali could make a simple picture list by the door so he can check the steps himself.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel when Bhupen mixes up the hand-washing?
qa.a: Sonali seems amused and patient, laughing and helping him sort it out.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young child working through a sequence of steps before going to the park with some prompting.

passage:

For weeks, Irawati (five) needed three reminders at home time: shoes, bag, water bottle.
On Monday I stuck three small pictures by her hook: a shoe, a bag, a bottle.
Today she pointed at each picture and did each one, saying “Shoe. Bag. Bottle.” She was ready first. She told me, “I did all by myself!”

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when she was ready first?

qa.q: How might Irawati's parents feel reading this note?

passage:
In their small town in Assam, the school van honked outside at 7:40.
Ritu, five, had a routine: shoes, bag, water bottle. She put on her shoes. She grabbed her bag. She ran to the door.
Then she stopped. “Bottle!”
She ran back to the kitchen table, grabbed it, and ran out.
Bidisha watched from the verandah. She hadn't said a word.
Ritu waved from the van, holding up the bottle.

qa.q: What time did the van honk?
qa.a: The school van honked at 7:40.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when she remembered her bottle?
qa.a: She felt a moment of worry and then pride as she ran back to get it.

qa.q: Why was it helpful that Bidisha didn't remind Ritu?
qa.a: It let Ritu remember the last step herself, strengthening her routine.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel watching Ritu wave with the bottle?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and pleased that Ritu managed the routine alone.

grounding: A five-year-old completes her morning routine and remembers a step without a reminder.

passage:
In Mexico City, Alejandro sang the going-out song while he tied his own shoes. “Jacket, hat, and snack in bag!”
Nadia, five, sang it back. She pulled on her jacket, zipped it halfway, then all the way. She put on her hat. She looked around.
“Snack!”
She took the banana from the table and put it in her bag.
“Ready, Papá!”
Alejandro opened the door. “Park, here we come.”

qa.q: What was Nadia's snack?
qa.a: A banana from the table.

qa.q: How did Nadia feel when she said “Ready, Papá!”?
qa.a: She felt proud and excited to have done all the steps herself.

qa.q: Why was singing the going-out song helpful?
qa.a: The song put the steps in order, so Nadia could remember each one.

qa.q: How might Alejandro feel when Nadia is ready by herself?
qa.a: He probably feels pleased and proud, and happy they can leave quickly.

grounding: A five-year-old follows a sung three-step routine to get ready for the park.

passage:
At the end of the day in the preschool, Miss Kaur rang the little bell. "Pack-up time."
Pooja pushed in her chair. Lunchbox in the bag. Water bottle… she looked around. It was under the table. Into the bag.
Shoes next. She sat and pulled them on, left then right.
Gargi was still colouring. Pooja tapped her. "Chair, box, bottle, shoes!"
Gargi jumped up.
Miss Kaur looked over. Pooja was already standing in line, bag on her back, without a single reminder.

qa.a: Under the table.

qa.q: What does Pooja tapping Gargi suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: Pooja feels confident and proud about knowing the routine, and wants to help Gargi too.

qa.q: What could Miss Kaur do to support Pooja and Gargi?
qa.a: Miss Kaur could name Pooja's steps with a smile and let Pooja keep saying the list for friends who need it.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel when Pooja reminds her?
qa.a: Gargi might be a little startled but glad of the help, since she had forgotten while colouring.

grounding: A preschooler completes her pack-up routine with no reminders and helps a friend.

passage:
I'm Elizabeth, and I live upstairs from Kishore. In winter mornings I see him through their open door.
His mother stuck a picture chart on the wall: a sweater, shoes, a bag, a water bottle.
In December, Kishore stood in front of the chart and touched each picture. Sweater on. Shoes on. He grabbed the bag and nearly ran out. Then he stopped, went back, touched the last picture, and fetched the bottle.
His mother only said, "Ready?" He was.
I can't say what he was thinking, but he looked very pleased.

qa.q: What four pictures were on the chart?
qa.a: A sweater, shoes, a bag and a water bottle.

qa.q: What might Kishore have been feeling when he went back for the bottle?
qa.a: Kishore probably felt a flash of worry, then relief and pride at catching the missing step himself.

qa.q: Why does the picture chart suit Kishore?
qa.a: It lets him check each step on his own instead of waiting for his mother to remind him.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Kishore's mornings?
qa.a: Elizabeth watches from outside and isn't sure what he thinks, but sees him finish the routine and look pleased.

grounding: A neighbour watches a young child use a picture chart to follow his morning routine.

passage:
The first monsoon week, Manoj forgot his raincoat twice and his bottle once. Amandeep, his mother, reminded him at the door each time.
The next week she made up a song: "Raincoat, bag, and bottle, then the shoes go on!" Manoj sang it every morning, loudly, and forgot only the bottle once.
By the end of the month, Amandeep was still in the kitchen when Manoj shouted, "Raincoat, bag, bottle, shoes! Done!" He stood at the door, ready, the hood already up.

qa.q: What did Manoj forget twice in the first monsoon week?
qa.a: His raincoat.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when he shouted "Done!"?
qa.a: Manoj felt proud and excited to be ready all by himself.

qa.q: Why did the song help Manoj?
qa.a: The song put the steps in order and made them easy to remember, so he needed fewer reminders.

qa.q: What is it like for Amandeep by the end of the month?
qa.a: Amandeep can stay in the kitchen and feels relieved 😊 that the mornings are easier.

grounding: Over the monsoon weeks a child learns his morning routine with the help of a song.

passage:
Class note, UKG, first week of the monsoon. Written by Himani, class teacher.
Mridul, five, used to stand at the door at home time, forgetting what came next. This week, with rain, the list is longer: raincoat, shoes, bag, water bottle, umbrella.
I stuck picture cards by the hooks. On Monday he needed three reminders. By Thursday he looked at the cards, did all five, and said to his friend Kabir, "Your bottle! You forgot!" Kabir went back for it.
Next: I'll take one card away and see if he remembers.

qa.q: What were the five things on the monsoon list?
qa.a: Raincoat, shoes, bag, water bottle and umbrella.

qa.q: How can you tell Mridul felt confident about the routine by Thursday?
qa.a: He did all five steps with no help and even reminded his friend Kabir, which shows he felt sure and proud.

qa.q: Which step helped Mridul most, and why?
qa.a: The picture cards by the hooks helped because they showed each step, so he could follow the order without an adult telling him.

qa.q: How might Kabir feel when Mridul reminds him about the bottle?
qa.a: Kabir might feel a little surprised but grateful, since Mridul's reminder saved him from leaving it behind.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to follow a multi-step routine with fewer reminders.
